He said: 'Then what brought you here?' He said: 'I came so that you might teach me something I can say when I go to sleep.' * *

So Allah revealed this surah, and in it commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to disassociate himself completely from their religion. He said: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾, meaning the idols and rivals, ﴿nor do you worship what I worship﴾, which is Allah alone, without partner. Here "mā" (what) carries the meaning of "man" (who).

Then He said: ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped, nor will you be worshippers of what I worship﴾, that is, I do not worship in the manner of your worship; I do not follow it or imitate it, but I worship Allah in the way that He loves and approves. For this reason He said: ﴿nor will you be worshippers of what I worship﴾, that is, you do not follow the commands of Allah and His legislation in His worship, but rather you have invented something of your own accord, as He said: ﴿They follow only conjecture and what their souls desire, and there has already come to them guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 23]. So He disassociated Himself from them in all that they are engaged in, for the worshipper must have a object of worship that he worships, and a way of worship by which he approaches it. The Messenger and his followers worship Allah by what He has legislated. For this reason the word of Islam is "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," meaning: there is no one worthy of worship except Allah, and there is no path to Him except by what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought. The polytheists worship other than Allah in a manner that Allah has not permitted. For this reason the Messenger (ﷺ) said to them: ﴿To you is your religion, and to me is my religion﴾, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if they deny you, say: "For me is my deed, and for you is your deed. He did not say "dini" (my religion) with a yā' because the verse ends with a nūn, so the yā' is elided, as He said: ﴿so He guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 78] and ﴿and He cures me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 80]. Others said: "I do not worship what you worship now, and I will not answer you for the rest of my life, nor will you be worshippers of what I worship." These are the ones of whom He said: ﴿And what has been sent down to you from your Lord will certainly increase many of them in rebellion and disbelief﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64].

End of what he mentioned.¹⁴

Indeed, with hardship there is ease﴾ [al-Sharh: 5-6], and like His saying: ﴿You will surely see the Hellfire; then you will surely see it with certainty of sight﴾ [al-Takathur: 6-7]. It is firmly established in Sahih Muslim, from Jabir, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited this surah and "Say: He is Allah, One" (﴿قُلْ هُوَ اللَّهُ أَحَدٌ﴾) in the two rak'ahs of the tawaf.² [Sahih Muslim, no. 1218, from the lengthy hadith on Jabir's famous account of the Hajj rites.]

In Sahih Muslim, from the hadith of Abu Hurairah, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited both of them in the two rak'ahs of Fajr.

Imam Ahmad said: Waki' related to us, Isra'il related to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Mujahid, from Ibn Umar, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited in the two rak'ahs before Fajr and the two rak'ahs after Maghrib, some twenty-odd times, or about ten-odd times, "Say: O you who disbelieve" and "Say: He is Allah, One."³

Ahmad also said: Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn al-Zubair related to us, Isra'il related to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Mujahid, from Ibn Umar, who said: "I watched the Prophet (ﷺ) twenty-four or twenty-five times, reciting in the two rak'ahs before Fajr and the two rak'ahs after Maghrib, 'Say: O you who disbelieve' and 'Say: He is Allah, One.'"⁴

Ahmad said: Abu Ahmad, namely Muhammad ibn Abdullah ibn al-Zubair al-Zubairi, related to us, Sufyan, namely al-Thawri, related to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Mujahid, from Ibn Umar, who said: "I watched the Prophet (ﷺ) for a month, and he would recite in the two rak'ahs before Fajr 'Say: O you who disbelieve' and 'Say: He is Allah, One.'"

It is similarly related by al-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah, through the hadith of Abu Ahmad al-Zubairi.⁵ al-Nasa'i related it through another route, from Abu Ishaq, with the same wording.⁶ al-Tirmidhi said: "This is a hasan hadith."

It has already been mentioned in a hadith that this surah is equal to a quarter of the Qur'an, and "When the earth is shaken" (Surah al-Zalzalah) is equal to a quarter of the Qur'an.

Imam Ahmad said: Hashim⁷ ibn al-Qasim related to us, Zuhair related to us, Abu Ishaq related to us, from Farwah ibn Nawfal, namely the son of Mu'awiyah, from his father, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to him: "Would you like a stepdaughter of ours whom you could look after?" He said: "I think she is Zainab." He said: "Then he came, and the Prophet (ﷺ) asked him about her. He said: 'What became of the girl?' He said: 'I left her with her mother.' He said: 'Then what brought you here?' He said: 'I came so that you might teach me something I can say when I go to sleep.' He said: 'Recite: "Say: O you who disbelieve," then sleep upon its end, for it is a declaration of freedom from shirk.'" Ahmad alone narrated it.⁸

Abu al-Qasim al-Tabarani said: Ahmad ibn Amr al-Qatrani related to us, Muhammad ibn al-Tufayl related to us, Sharik related to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Jabalah ibn Harithah, namely the brother of Zayd ibn Harithah, that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When you go to your bed, recite 'Say: O you who disbelieve' until you reach its end, for it is a declaration of freedom from shirk."⁹

Imam Ahmad said: Hajjaj related to us, Sharik related to us, from Abu Ishaq, from Farwah ibn Nawfal, from al-Harith ibn Jabalah, who said: "I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, teach me something to say when I go to sleep.' He said: 'When you lie down at night, recite "Say: O you who disbelieve," for it is a declaration of freedom from shirk.'"¹⁰

al-Tabarani narrated through the route of Sharik, from Jabir,¹¹ from Ma'qil al-Zubaydi, from [Abbad Abi al-Akhdar, from Khabbab],¹² that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite, when he lay down on his bed, "Say: O you who disbelieve," until he finished it.¹³

**In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful**

* *

This surah is the declaration of freedom from the worship that the polytheists practise, and it commands sincerity in it. His saying, ﴿Say: O you who disbelieve﴾, encompasses every disbeliever on the face of the earth, but those directly addressed by this address are the disbelievers of Quraysh.

It has been said that out of their ignorance they invited the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to worship their idols for one year, and they would worship his God for one year. So Allah revealed this surah, and in it commanded His Messenger (ﷺ) to disassociate himself completely from their religion. He said: ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾, meaning the idols and rivals, ﴿nor do you worship what I worship﴾, which is Allah alone, without partner. Here "mā" (what) carries the meaning of "man" (who).

Then He said: ﴿Nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped, nor will you be worshippers of what I worship﴾, that is, I do not worship in the manner of your worship; I do not follow it or imitate it, but I worship Allah in the way that He loves and approves. For this reason He said: ﴿nor will you be worshippers of what I worship﴾, that is, you do not follow the commands of Allah and His legislation in His worship, but rather you have invented something of your own accord, as He said: ﴿They follow only conjecture and what their souls desire, and there has already come to them guidance from their Lord﴾ [al-Najm: 23]. So He disassociated Himself from them in all that they are engaged in, for the worshipper must have a object of worship that he worships, and a way of worship by which he approaches it. The Messenger and his followers worship Allah by what He has legislated. For this reason the word of Islam is "There is no god but Allah, Muhammad is the Messenger of Allah," meaning: there is no one worthy of worship except Allah, and there is no path to Him except by what the Messenger (ﷺ) brought. The polytheists worship other than Allah in a manner that Allah has not permitted. For this reason the Messenger (ﷺ) said to them: ﴿To you is your religion, and to me is my religion﴾, as Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if they deny you, say: "For me is my deed, and for you is your deed. You are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do"﴾ [Yunus: 41], and He said: ﴿For us are our deeds, and for you are your deeds﴾ [al-Qasas: 55].

al-Bukhari said: It is said that ﴿your religion﴾ is disbelief, and ﴿my religion﴾ is Islam. He did not say "dini" (my religion) with a yā' because the verse ends with a nūn, so the yā' is elided, as He said: ﴿so He guides me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 78] and ﴿and He cures me﴾ [al-Shu'ara: 80]. Others said: "I do not worship what you worship now, and I will not answer you for the rest of my life, nor will you be worshippers of what I worship." These are the ones of whom He said: ﴿And what has been sent down to you from your Lord will certainly increase many of them in rebellion and disbelief﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 64].

End of what he mentioned.¹⁴

Ibn Jarir transmitted from some of the Arabic grammarians that this is a case of emphasis, like His saying: ﴿So indeed, with hardship there is ease. Indeed, with hardship there is ease﴾ [al-Sharh: 5-6], and like His saying: ﴿You will surely see the Hellfire; then you will surely see it with certainty of sight﴾ [al-Takathur: 6-7]. Some of them, such as Ibn al-Jawzi and others, related it from Ibn Qutaybah. And Allah knows best. So there are three opinions: the first is what we mentioned at the outset. The second is what al-Bukhari and other exegetes related, that what is meant by ﴿I do not worship what you worship, nor will you be worshippers of what I worship﴾ refers to the past, and ﴿nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped, nor will you be worshippers of what I worship﴾ refers to the future. The third is that it is pure emphasis.

There is a fourth opinion, supported by Abu al-Abbas ibn Taymiyyah in some of his books, which is that what is meant by His saying ﴿I do not worship what you worship﴾ is the negation of the act, since it is a verbal sentence; and ﴿nor am I a worshipper of what you have worshipped﴾ is the negation of his being receptive to that at all, since negation by a nominal sentence is more emphatic. So it is as if he negated the act and also negated his capacity for it, which means negation of occurrence and negation of legal possibility. This too is a good opinion, and Allah knows best.

Imam Abu Abdullah al-Shafi'i and others have used this noble verse, ﴿To you is your religion, and to me is my religion﴾, as evidence that all disbelief is one religion, such that Jews inherit from Christians and vice versa, when there is between them a lineage or a cause through which inheritance passes, because all religions other than Islam are like a single thing in falsehood. Ahmad ibn Hanbal and those who agreed with him held that Christians do not inherit from Jews, nor Jews from Christians, based on the hadith of Amr ibn Shu'ayb, from his father, from his grandfather, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The people of two different religions do not inherit from one another."¹⁵

End of the tafsir of the surah "Say: O you who disbelieve," and to Allah belong all praise and grace.
